h1: How Insurance Umpires Are Chosen in Texas
secondary_keywords: how insurance umpires are chosen in Texas
excerpt: Texas insurance umpires are usually chosen by the two appraisers, or by a court if they deadlock. Learn the steps, umpire qualifications, fees and what umpires decide.
key_takeaways: The two appraisers usually choose the insurance umpire together.
If they cannot agree, often within 15 days, a Texas court can appoint one.
Umpires decide only items the appraisers cannot resolve.

body_html:
In Texas, an insurance umpire is usually chosen by the two appraisers in an appraisal, one appointed by the policyholder and one by the insurer. If they cannot agree within the time the policy allows, often 15 days, either side can ask a Texas court to appoint the umpire. The umpire then decides only the items the appraisers cannot resolve.

What is an insurance umpire?

An insurance umpire is a neutral third party in the appraisal process. Most Texas property policies, both homeowners and commercial, contain an appraisal clause that creates a three-person panel: the policyholder's appraiser, the insurer's appraiser and the umpire.

The two appraisers do most of the work. They inspect the property, prepare estimates and try to agree on the amount of loss. The umpire steps in when they cannot agree on some or all items. An award signed by any two of the three panel members sets the amount of loss.

That makes the insurance umpire the tie-breaker, and often the single most influential person in a disputed claim. For a deeper look at the role itself, see what an insurance umpire does.

How insurance umpires are chosen in Texas, step by step

The exact process depends on your policy's appraisal clause, so always read it. A typical Texas appraisal follows these steps:

  1. Appraisal is invoked. The policyholder or the insurer sends a written demand for appraisal.
  2. Each side names its appraiser. Most clauses require each party to choose a competent, disinterested appraiser within a set period, commonly 20 days.
  3. The appraisers exchange umpire candidates. Each appraiser proposes one or more names. They review qualifications, availability and potential conflicts.
  4. The appraisers agree on an umpire. Once both accept a candidate, the umpire is contacted, confirms availability and discloses any conflicts.
  5. If they cannot agree, a court appoints one. Many policies say that if the appraisers fail to agree within 15 days, either party may ask a judge of a court of record in the state where the property is located to select the umpire.
  6. The umpire is engaged. The umpire sets expectations for communication, scheduling, submissions and fees.

Some policies require the appraisers to pick an umpire before they begin appraising. Others allow them to appraise first and choose an umpire only if they reach an impasse. Read your clause carefully, because the timing affects how the process unfolds.

When a Texas court appoints the umpire

Court appointment is the fallback when the appraisers deadlock. In Texas, this usually means one party files a petition or application in a court with jurisdiction, asking the judge to name an umpire. Each side may propose candidates, and the judge selects one.

Court appointment adds time and cost, so most appraisers try hard to avoid it. It is still an important safeguard. It prevents either side from stalling the process indefinitely by refusing every reasonable candidate.

Common reasons appraisers fail to agree include:

  • Concern that a proposed umpire works mostly for carriers or mostly for policyholders
  • Lack of relevant experience, such as commercial roofing or large fire losses
  • Undisclosed relationships with a party, a contractor or an attorney
  • Scheduling or fee issues

If appraisers cannot agree on the umpire or on the amount of loss, the process can stall. Our article on what happens if appraisers disagree explains how those situations are resolved, including what happens at an impasse. This is general information, not legal advice.

What makes a good insurance umpire?

Policies rarely spell out umpire qualifications beyond requiring someone competent and impartial. In practice, appraisers look for:

QualityWhy it matters
ImpartialityThe umpire must be fair to both sides and free of conflicts that could undermine the award
Construction and estimating knowledgeDisputes turn on scope, repair methods and pricing in Xactimate or Symbility
Claim-type experienceRoof, water, fire and commercial losses each require specific technical understanding
Knowledge of Texas appraisal rulesThe umpire must stay within the amount-of-loss role and avoid deciding coverage
Clear communicationBoth appraisers need to understand what evidence the umpire wants and how decisions will be explained
AvailabilityA highly qualified umpire who cannot inspect for months slows the entire claim

Umpires come from several backgrounds, including experienced appraisers, public and independent adjusters, contractors, engineers and sometimes attorneys or retired judges. Background matters less than fairness, technical skill and a disciplined process.

What an insurance umpire can and cannot decide

Texas law sets clear limits on the appraisal panel. Under State Farm Lloyds v. Johnson (Tex. 2009), appraisers and umpires decide the amount of loss. They may consider the extent of damage and causation as part of that job, but they do not decide coverage or liability.

In practice, an insurance umpire may decide:

  • How many roof slopes need replacement
  • Whether drywall must be replaced or can be repaired
  • Appropriate unit prices and quantities
  • Whether damage was caused by the claimed storm versus wear, when that is part of the amount-of-loss dispute
  • Replacement cost and actual cash value figures

The umpire should not decide whether the policy covers a loss, whether an exclusion applies or whether the insurer acted in bad faith. Those questions stay with the parties and, if necessary, the courts. Awards are generally binding on the amount of loss, as discussed in our article is insurance appraisal legally binding in Texas.

How the umpire works once chosen

Once appointed, the umpire's job is narrow and specific. A typical process looks like this:

  1. The appraisers settle every item they can agree on.
  2. They identify the remaining disputed items and submit them to the umpire with their estimates and supporting evidence.
  3. The umpire reviews submissions and, in many cases, inspects the property with both appraisers.
  4. The umpire may ask questions, request more documentation or hold a joint meeting.
  5. The umpire decides each disputed item and signs an award with whichever appraiser agrees.
Tip: The umpire decides based on evidence, not volume. A clear, organized submission with photos, measurements, code citations and pricing support for each disputed line item is far more persuasive than a long narrative.

Tips for policyholders during umpire selection

As a policyholder, you usually do not pick the insurance umpire yourself. Your appraiser does that work. You can still help the process go smoothly and protect your interests.

Ask your appraiser how they evaluate candidates

A good appraiser will explain what they look for in an umpire, which candidates they plan to propose and why. Ask whether a proposed umpire has relevant experience with your type of loss, such as hail-damaged roofs, water losses or commercial buildings.

Watch the deadlines

Policy deadlines for naming appraisers and umpires matter. If the other side's appraiser is slow to respond, your appraiser can document the delay and, if needed, move toward court appointment. Keep copies of every letter and email about the selection process.

Insist on disclosure

Ask that any umpire candidate disclose prior work with either party, either appraiser or any attorney or contractor involved in the claim. Disclosure up front prevents disputes later about whether the umpire was impartial.

Keep your evidence ready

Umpire selection is a good time to finish organizing photos, estimates, invoices and expert reports. Once the umpire is in place, disputed items can move quickly if the evidence is already assembled.

How long does umpire selection take?

When the appraisers cooperate, choosing an umpire often takes a few days to a couple of weeks. When they deadlock and a court must appoint one, it can take considerably longer, depending on the court's schedule. Prompt, reasonable proposals from both appraisers are the best way to keep the overall appraisal timeline on track.

Insurance umpire fees and who pays

Under most appraisal clauses, each party pays its own appraiser and the umpire's fee is split equally between the policyholder and the insurer. Umpires may charge hourly, a flat fee or a fee tied to the complexity of the claim. Ask about the fee structure before the umpire is engaged so nobody is surprised.

Court appointment can add filing and related costs on top of the umpire's fee, which is another reason appraisers usually try to agree on their own.

Keep the umpire fee in perspective. On a claim where the appraisers are far apart, a fair and well-reasoned umpire decision is usually worth far more than the shared cost of getting it. Our appraisal cost calculator can help you weigh appraisal costs against the amount in dispute.

Insurance umpire services across Texas

Appraisals happen everywhere Texas weather does damage: hail in Dallas, Fort Worth, Plano and Frisco; wind and hail in Austin, Round Rock and Waco; hurricanes in Houston, Galveston and Corpus Christi; and Panhandle hail in Amarillo and Lubbock. Umpires are often needed in each of these markets, and appraisers frequently look for umpires who know local construction practices and pricing.

That appraiser will propose and evaluate umpire candidates on your behalf, present your evidence and negotiate the award. faqs.q: Who selects the insurance umpire in a Texas appraisal?
faqs.a: The two appraisers, one chosen by the policyholder and one by the insurer, normally select the umpire together. If they cannot agree within the time the policy sets, often 15 days, either party can ask a court of record in the state where the property is located to appoint the umpire.

faqs.q: Can I object to a proposed insurance umpire?
faqs.a: Yes. Your appraiser can decline a proposed umpire because of conflicts, lack of relevant experience or availability problems. If the appraisers cannot agree on anyone, a court may appoint the umpire. Raise concerns about impartiality early, since challenging an umpire after an award is much harder.

faqs.q: How much does an insurance umpire cost in Texas?
faqs.a: Umpire fees vary by experience, claim size and complexity. Some umpires bill hourly while others charge a flat or tiered fee. Most appraisal clauses split the umpire fee equally between the policyholder and the insurer. Confirm the fee arrangement in writing before the umpire begins work.

faqs.q: Does the umpire have to inspect the property?
faqs.a: Not always, but many umpires do, especially on roof and structural disputes where photos alone may not settle the question. The umpire may inspect with both appraisers present, review estimates and evidence, and ask follow-up questions before deciding each disputed item.

faqs.q: Is the insurance umpire decision final?
faqs.a: An award signed by the umpire and one appraiser is generally binding on the amount of loss in Texas. Courts set awards aside only in limited situations, such as fraud, accident, mistake, or an award that goes beyond the panel’s authority. Coverage questions remain separate from the award.

faqs.q: Can a public adjuster or contractor serve as an umpire?
faqs.a: Umpires come from various backgrounds, including appraisers, adjusters, contractors and engineers. What matters most is impartiality and competence. A person with a financial interest in the claim, such as the contractor doing the repairs, would not be an appropriate umpire for that loss.
